title: Binary Search
description: Finds a target value in a sorted array by repeatedly halving the search space. At each step, compare the target to the middle element and discard the half that cannot contain the target.
key_insight: Requires data to be sorted. Each comparison eliminates half the remaining candidates. Works on any monotone predicate, not just arrays.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to verify precondition (sorted input)
Off-by-one in mid = (lo + hi) // 2 — use lo + (hi - lo) // 2 to avoid integer overflow in C/Java
Infinite loop when lo and hi are adjacent and update logic is wrong
code_template:
lo, hi = 0, len(arr) - 1
while lo <= hi:
    mid = lo + (hi - lo) // 2
    if arr[mid] == target: return mid
    elif arr[mid] < target: lo = mid + 1
    else: hi = mid - 1
return -1

title: Merge Sort
description: Stable, comparison-based sort. Recursively divides the array in half, sorts each half, then merges the two sorted halves. Guarantees O(n log n) in all cases.
use_cases: sorting linked lists (no random access needed)
key_insight: Merge step is O(n) and there are O(log n) levels — hence O(n log n) total. The extra O(n) space is required for the merge buffer.
common_mistakes: Not allocating extra space for merge buffer
Forgetting to copy back from temporary array
Off-by-one in merge loop termination

title: Quick Sort
description: In-place, comparison-based sort. Picks a pivot, partitions array so elements < pivot are left, > pivot are right, then recursively sorts both sides. Fast in practice due to cache efficiency.
use_cases: faster than merge sort in practice for in-memory data
key_insight: Pivot choice is critical. Random pivot or median-of-three avoids worst-case O(n²) on sorted input. Lomuto partition is simpler; Hoare partition is faster.
common_mistakes: Using first element as pivot on already-sorted input (triggers O(n²))
Not randomising pivot
Confusion between Lomuto and Hoare partition invariants

title: Dijkstra's Shortest Path
description: Finds the shortest path from a source node to all other nodes in a weighted graph with non-negative edge weights. Uses a min-heap to always extend the cheapest known path.

complexity.time_best: O((V + E) log V) with binary heap
complexity.time_worst: O(V²) with adjacency matrix / no heap

key_insight: Works only with non-negative weights. Negative weights require Bellman-Ford. The greedy invariant: once a node is popped from the heap, its shortest distance is final.
common_mistakes: Using with negative edge weights (gives wrong answer)
Forgetting to skip already-visited nodes when using lazy deletion
Not initialising distances to infinity

title: Breadth-First Search (BFS)
description: Explores a graph level by level from a source node using a queue. Finds the shortest path (fewest edges) in unweighted graphs.
key_insight: Uses FIFO queue. All nodes at distance k are processed before any node at distance k+1. This guarantees minimum-hop shortest paths.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to mark nodes as visited before enqueuing (causes exponential blowup)
Confusing BFS (queue) with DFS (stack/recursion)

title: Depth-First Search (DFS)
description: Explores as far as possible along each branch before backtracking. Can be implemented recursively (call stack) or iteratively (explicit stack).
key_insight: DFS explores depth-first, which means it may find very long paths early. Use BFS for shortest paths in unweighted graphs; use DFS for reachability, cycle detection, and topological ordering.
common_mistakes: Stack overflow on deep recursion (use iterative DFS for large graphs)
Forgetting visited set in cyclic graphs (infinite loop)

title: 0/1 Knapsack (Dynamic Programming)
description: Given n items each with a weight and value, find the maximum total value that fits in a knapsack of capacity W. Each item can be taken (1) or left (0).
key_insight: State: dp[w] = max value using capacity w. Transition: dp[w] = max(dp[w], dp[w - weight[i]] + value[i]). Iterate items outer, capacity inner (in reverse to avoid reuse).
common_mistakes: Iterating capacity in forward order (turns into unbounded knapsack)
Using 2D array when O(W) rolling array suffices
Not handling w < weight[i] edge case

title: Longest Common Subsequence (LCS)
description: Finds the longest subsequence common to two sequences. A subsequence preserves relative order but need not be contiguous.
key_insight: dp[i][j] = length of LCS of first i chars of A and first j chars of B. If A[i]==B[j]: dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1. Otherwise: dp[i][j] = max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]).

title: Fibonacci (Memoisation vs Tabulation)
description: Classic intro to DP. Naive recursion is O(2^n). Memoisation (top-down) and tabulation (bottom-up) reduce to O(n). Space-optimised bottom-up uses O(1).
key_insight: Memoisation = recursion + cache. Tabulation = fill table iteratively. Both are O(n) time. Space-optimised uses only prev two values.
code_template:
# O(n) time, O(1) space
def fib(n):
    a, b = 0, 1
    for _ in range(n): a, b = b, a + b
    return a

title: Union-Find (Disjoint Set Union)
description: Tracks a partition of elements into disjoint sets. Supports two operations: find (which set does this element belong to?) and union (merge two sets). With path compression and union by rank, both are near O(1) amortised.
key_insight: Path compression flattens the tree during find. Union by rank keeps the tree shallow. Together they give inverse-Ackermann O(α(n)) per operation — effectively constant.

title: Two Pointers Technique
description: Uses two indices that move through a data structure (usually an array or string) to solve problems in O(n) that naïve approaches solve in O(n²). Both pointers typically start at different ends or move at different speeds.
key_insight: Works when the problem has a monotone structure — advancing one pointer improves the answer in a predictable direction. Requires sorted input for many applications.
common_mistakes: Applying to unsorted array when sorted is required
Confusing two-pointer with sliding window (window uses a maintained size constraint)

title: Sliding Window
description: Maintains a window (contiguous subarray/substring) and slides it across the input to find optimal/valid windows in O(n). The window expands by moving the right pointer and shrinks by moving the left pointer.

complexity.space: O(k) where k is window size or alphabet size

use_cases: maximum sum subarray of size k
count subarrays with given sum (fixed window)
key_insight: For fixed-size windows: move both pointers together. For variable-size windows: expand right pointer until constraint is violated, then shrink left pointer until valid again. Each element enters and leaves the window at most once.

title: Topological Sort (Kahn's / DFS)
description: Linear ordering of nodes in a directed acyclic graph (DAG) such that for every directed edge u→v, node u appears before v. Used to find valid orderings of dependent tasks.
key_insight: Only defined for DAGs. Kahn's algorithm: repeatedly remove nodes with in-degree 0. If any nodes remain at the end, there's a cycle. DFS approach: add node to result stack on the post-visit.
common_mistakes: Applying to a graph with cycles (no valid topological order exists)
Forgetting that the result is not unique — multiple valid orderings may exist

title: RSA Public-Key Cryptography
description: Asymmetric encryption scheme based on the difficulty of factoring large composite numbers. A public key (n, e) encrypts; a private key (n, d) decrypts. Security relies on factoring n = p×q being computationally infeasible.
use_cases: secure key exchange for symmetric encryption
key_insight: Never use RSA directly for large data — use it to encrypt a symmetric key (AES), then encrypt data with AES. Use OAEP padding, never textbook RSA. Minimum 2048-bit keys; prefer 4096-bit.
common_mistakes: Using textbook RSA without padding (vulnerable to many attacks)
Using RSA for bulk encryption (too slow)
Reusing key pairs across different security domains

title: Hash Table (Hash Map)
description: Maps keys to values using a hash function. Average O(1) insert, lookup, and delete. Handles collisions via chaining (linked list buckets) or open addressing (probe sequence).
key_insight: Load factor (n/m where n=entries, m=buckets) should stay below 0.7 to maintain O(1) average. Python dict and Java HashMap handle this automatically via rehashing.
common_mistakes: Using mutable objects as keys (they must be hashable/immutable)
Assuming iteration order (before Python 3.7, dict was unordered)

title: Binary Heap / Priority Queue
description: Complete binary tree maintaining the heap property: parent ≤ children (min-heap) or parent ≥ children (max-heap). Supports efficient insert (O(log n)) and extract-min/max (O(log n)). Array representation: parent of i is (i-1)//2; children are 2i+1 and 2i+2.
key_insight: Python's heapq is a min-heap. For max-heap, negate values. heapify converts a list to heap in O(n) — faster than n × O(log n) individual inserts.
code_template:
import heapq
heap = []
heapq.heappush(heap, val)   # O(log n)
val = heapq.heappop(heap)    # O(log n) min
val = heap[0]                # O(1) peek
heapq.heapify(lst)           # O(n) in-place

title: Trie (Prefix Tree)
description: Tree data structure for storing strings. Each node represents a character. Root-to-node path spells out a prefix. Efficient for prefix search, autocomplete, and word existence checks.
key_insight: Insert, search, and startsWith are all O(m) where m is word length — independent of vocabulary size. More memory-efficient alternatives: compressed tries (Patricia trie), or hash-map children instead of fixed array.

title: Segment Tree
description: Binary tree over an array that allows range queries (sum, min, max) and point updates in O(log n). The tree is built bottom-up; each internal node stores the aggregate of its range.
use_cases: range sum query with point updates
key_insight: Build in O(n). Each query decomposes into O(log n) disjoint ranges. Lazy propagation extends to range updates in O(log n). Simpler alternative for static range min: sparse table (O(1) query, O(n log n) build).

title: Knuth-Morris-Pratt (KMP) String Search
description: Finds all occurrences of a pattern P in text T in O(n + m) time by precomputing a failure function that avoids re-examining already-matched characters.
key_insight: The failure function lps[i] = length of longest proper prefix of P[0..i] that is also a suffix. When mismatch occurs, shift pattern by lps[j-1] instead of 1 — no need to restart from text position.

title: QuickSelect — Kth Smallest/Largest
description: Selection algorithm to find the kth smallest (or largest) element in an unsorted array in average O(n) time. Uses the partition step from QuickSort but recurses into only one side.
use_cases: top-k elements (combine with heap for k << n)
key_insight: After partitioning: if pivot index == k, we're done. If pivot index > k, recurse left; else recurse right. Median-of-medians gives guaranteed O(n) worst case but is complex.
